title: Anthropic migrated its Messages API from a Python monolith to Rust with Claude writing most of the code
subtitle: On the Latent Space podcast, platform-engineering lead Katelyn Lesse said the team had no Rust developers at the start and gave rough figures of 40–50 percent lower CPU and 10–20 percent faster time to first token after cutover.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Anthropic's Messages API — the HTTP endpoint behind every Claude request from a model-using application — now runs on a Rust service, not the Python monolith it started on. Katelyn Lesse, who runs platform engineering at Anthropic, described the migration on the Latent Space podcast episode published October 27. She said the previous system had, in her own words, very low CPU efficiency, and that the team chose Rust despite having no Rust developers on it at the start. Claude wrote most of the new service. The old and new systems were run in parallel on shadow traffic before the cutover.

The reported gains are rough. Lesse put them at about 40 to 50 percent less CPU per request and 10 to 20 percent faster time to first token in some cases. Those figures came from a conversational answer, not a published benchmark, and secondary coverage disagrees on whether they came from production measurement or from the team's estimates. There is no Anthropic engineering post yet to cite, no comparative latency distribution, and no breakdown of which portion of the gain came from Rust versus from restructuring a monolith with acknowledged inefficiencies.

What is unambiguous is the operating pattern. A frontier lab let its own model do the heavy lifting on a core production rewrite, in a language the team did not already know, against a service that handles traffic for every paying customer. That is a stronger self-use claim than any public demo — and it comes a week after Anthropic's separate post on using Claude Code to port Bun's million-line codebase from Zig to Rust in roughly two weeks. Both are examples of what large-scale coding-agent use actually looks like inside the lab shipping the agent.

A note for learners: when a company reports a performance win from an AI-driven rewrite, do the math on what was replaced. A Python service already described as inefficient will yield large gains in any strongly-typed, compiled rewrite — Rust, Go, C++ — because the comparison baseline was soft. The story worth watching is not the CPU number; it is the ratio of human engineer time to shipped code and the defect rate after cutover. Those are what will determine whether other teams can copy this approach, and neither has been published yet.
